claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 has a high-temperature BCC state.
The high-temperature BCC state of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is metastable.
Slow cooling provides enough time for diffusional elemental partitioning in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Al is the primary partitioning or segregating element during cooling of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Elemental partitioning creates local compositional fluctuations that nucleate secondary FCC or intermetallic phases from the BCC matrix.
Elemental partitioning drives coarsening of the secondary phases.
Rapid quenching suppresses diffusion and thereby preserves the high-temperature BCC structure.
The relevant phase stability is governed by kinetic competition between diffusion-mediated transformation and quench retention.
Segregation lowers the local free energy sufficiently to favor nucleation of secondary phases.
Relative to a quenched baseline, slow-cooled samples will have a higher secondary-phase volume fraction.
Relative to a quenched baseline, slow-cooled samples will have a coarser secondary-phase microstructure.
Slow cooling will produce measurable lattice-parameter shifts relative to rapid quenching.
Slow cooling will produce measurable local-composition changes relative to rapid quenching.
A rapid quench provides a baseline that retains the metastable BCC state.
The proposed mechanism should dominate at slow-to-moderate cooling rates where diffusion is appreciable.
The proposed transformation mechanism should not operate during extremely rapid cooling because diffusion time is insufficient.
Significant mechanical deformation may alter diffusion kinetics and invalidate the proposed cooling-rate mechanism.
The exact quantitative relationship among cooling rate, diffusion time, and secondary-phase formation is unknown and may depend on minor alloying effects.
A lack of statistically significant differences in secondary-phase fraction, coarsening, and local composition between slow-cooled and quenched samples would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The conditions state that both quenched and slow-cooled sets receive the same isothermal holds, but the detailed design explicitly assigns the 700–800 °C holds only to the slow-cooled group. The latter design confounds cooling history with thermal exposure.

The baseline is defined as an immediately quenched specimen retaining BCC, while the conditions say the baseline also undergoes isothermal exposure. A post-hold quenched specimen may no longer represent the stated as-quenched BCC baseline.
